slides.title: From World War II to 1948 Arab-Israeli War
slides.cap: UN partition plan and the strategic geography of the 1947-1948 civil-war phase
slides.body: World War II transformed the political future of Mandatory Palestine. The Holocaust intensified demands for a Jewish state, Britain withdrew from the mandate, and the United Nations proposed partition. The declaration of Israel and rejection of partition by neighboring Arab states led directly to war in 1948.

stats.lbl: World War II transformed the political future of Mandatory Palestine. The Holocaust intensified demands for a Jewish state, Britain withdrew from the mandate, and the United Nations proposed partition. The declaration of Israel and rejection of partition by neighboring Arab states led directly to war in 1948.

slides.title: The Civil War Begins
slides.cap: UN partition plan and the strategic geography of the 1947-1948 civil-war phase
slides.body:
After the United Nations voted to partition Mandatory Palestine into Jewish and Arab states, Arab leaders rejected the plan and fighting began almost immediately. Jewish neighborhoods, roads, and convoys came under attack while the Yishuv prepared to defend the future state before the British withdrawal. The Haganah moved from local defense toward coordinated operations, while the Palmach protected isolated settlements and vital routes.

The civil-war phase forced the Yishuv to build a functioning army under fire. It showed that the state approved by diplomacy would still have to be secured by soldiers, supply convoys, local defense, and control of the roads linking Jewish population centers.

stats.lbl: Jewish forces fought without a sovereign state
The civil-war phase forced the Yishuv to build a functioning army under fire and demonstrated that the Jewish state would have to be secured militarily, not merely approved diplomatically.

slides.title: The Battle for Jerusalem
slides.body:
Jerusalem was home to roughly 100,000 Jews, but the road connecting it to the coastal plain ran through hostile terrain and was repeatedly blocked by Arab forces. Jewish convoys carrying food, fuel, ammunition, and medicine suffered ambushes and heavy losses. Operations Nachshon and Maccabi fought to reopen the road, while the improvised Burma Road later bypassed the Arab Legion position at Latrun. For Israel, keeping Jewish Jerusalem alive became one of the war's most urgent military and national missions.

Holding and supplying Jewish Jerusalem prevented the city's surrender and made improvised logistics, convoy defense, and the Burma Road central symbols of Israeli endurance. this event helped determine whether the new state could defend its population, connect its territory, and emerge from invasion as a functioning sovereign country.

slides.title: Independence and Arab Invasion
slides.body:
David Ben-Gurion declared the establishment of the State of Israel on 14 May 1948 as the British Mandate ended. Within hours, armies from Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Lebanon, and Iraq entered the new state or the former Mandate territory. Israel began its independence facing a multi-front invasion while still merging the Haganah, Palmach, Irgun, and Lehi into a national army. the war was no longer only an intercommunal struggle: it was a fight to prevent the destruction of the newly declared Jewish state.

Israel survived the moment when its neighbors expected the new state to be defeated quickly, turning a declaration of independence into a durable political and military reality. this event helped determine whether the new state could defend its population, connect its territory, and emerge from invasion as a functioning sovereign country.

stats.lbl: Israel survived the moment when its neighbors expected the new state to be defeated quickly, turning a declaration of independence into a durable political and military reality.

markers.label: Burma Road
markers.description: Israeli engineers opened this bypass after direct attacks on Latrun failed.

slides.title: Battles of Latrun
slides.body: Latrun was one of the most painful and urgent struggles of the war. The Arab Legion held the fortress and junction controlling the main road from the coastal plain to Jerusalem. Jewish Jerusalem was isolated, short of food and supplies, and politically central to the new state. Israeli assaults on Latrun failed at heavy cost, including losses among newly arrived immigrants rushed into battle. Yet the failures forced Israel to improvise: engineers and soldiers opened the Burma Road, a bypass route that helped break the siege and keep Jewish Jerusalem alive. Although repeated assaults failed to capture the fortress, Israeli engineers and troops solved the strategic problem by opening the Burma Road around it.

stats.lbl: It preserved the fight for Jewish Jerusalem and pushed Israel to improvise under extreme pressure.

slides.title: The Wider Impact
slides.body: It preserved the fight for Jewish Jerusalem and pushed Israel to improvise under extreme pressure. Although repeated assaults failed to capture the fortress, Israeli engineers and troops solved the strategic problem by opening the Burma Road around it.

slides.title: Operation Pleshet
slides.body: Operation Pleshet was fought as an emergency action to stop the Egyptian Army from driving north along the coast. In late May 1948, Egyptian forces had advanced through the southern coastal plain and reached the Isdud area, close enough to threaten the road toward Tel Aviv and the center of the country. Israeli attacks did not fully destroy the Egyptian force, but they helped halt its advance. This mattered enormously: a continued Egyptian push north could have split Israeli territory and threatened the new state's most important urban center. The operation did not destroy the Egyptian army, but stopping its northward momentum helped protect Tel Aviv and bought Israel time to organize stronger forces.

stats.lbl: It helped prevent Egyptian forces from reaching Israel's central coastal heartland.

slides.title: Operation Danny
slides.body: Operation Danny was about securing the vulnerable heart of the new state. Tel Aviv, the coastal plain, and the road toward Jerusalem were under pressure, while Arab Legion positions and Palestinian irregular forces threatened movement between Jewish population centers. In July 1948, after the first truce ended, Israeli forces moved against Lydda and Ramle and tried to push eastward. The operation opened space around the Tel Aviv-Jerusalem corridor, but it also became one of the most controversial episodes of the war because of the flight and expulsion of many Arab residents from Lydda and Ramle. For Israel, the military gain was strategic depth; for Palestinians, it became part of the wider displacement remembered as the Nakba. The offensive was Israel's largest operation to that point and helped widen the protected corridor between the coastal heartland and Jerusalem.

stats.lbl: It strengthened Israel's central front and shaped both Israeli security geography and Palestinian memory of 1948.

slides.title: Operation Yoav
slides.body:
Operation Yoav was Israel's major October 1948 offensive in the south. Its goal was to break Egyptian pressure, reopen contact with isolated Israeli communities in the Negev, and shift the war from survival to initiative. Israeli forces attacked Egyptian positions across the southern front, opened corridors, and captured Beersheba. Yoav proved that the IDF had become more coordinated and capable than it had been in May. It also helped secure the Negev as part of Israel's future territory. The operation shifted the southern front in Israel's favor and opened the way toward Beersheba and the wider Negev.

It shifted the southern war in Israel's favor and helped anchor Israeli control of the Negev. The operation shifted the southern front in Israel's favor and opened the way toward Beersheba and the wider Negev.

slides.title: Operation Hiram
slides.body:
Operation Hiram was Israel's late October offensive in the Upper Galilee. Israeli commanders aimed to remove the remaining Arab Liberation Army presence, secure northern Jewish communities, and end the threat of a hostile enclave near the Lebanese border. The operation moved quickly and brought the Galilee under Israeli control. this secured the northern frontier; for many Arab communities, it meant displacement, flight, and a permanent change in the region's demography. In roughly sixty hours, Israeli forces secured the Upper Galilee and pushed the Arab Liberation Army away from Israel's northern communities.

It secured Israel's northern territory before the final armistice map took shape. In roughly sixty hours, Israeli forces secured the Upper Galilee and pushed the Arab Liberation Army away from Israel's northern communities.

slides.title: Operation Horev
slides.body:
Operation Horev was Israel's major winter offensive against the Egyptian army in the Negev. Israeli forces attacked fortified positions, cut supply routes, and maneuvered around Egyptian units, with some troops briefly crossing into Sinai before international pressure led them to withdraw. The operation broke Egypt's ability to continue offensive action and placed Israel in a strong position for armistice negotiations.

Operation Horev transformed the southern front from an Egyptian threat into an Israeli strategic advantage and pushed Egypt toward armistice negotiations.

markers.label: Umm Rashrash / Eilat
markers.description: The Ink Flag was raised here, giving Israel access to the Red Sea.

markers.label: Southern Negev
markers.description: Israeli columns moved through the Negev to establish control before the armistice map hardened.

slides.title: Operation Uvda
slides.body:
Operation Uvda was the final Israeli operation of the 1948 war. Israeli forces moved through the Negev toward Umm Rashrash, today Eilat, and raised the Ink Flag at the Red Sea. this was a symbolic and strategic conclusion: it linked the state to the Red Sea and demonstrated control over the southern Negev before the armistice map hardened. The operation involved little fighting compared with earlier battles, but its territorial significance was enormous. The almost bloodless advance ended with the improvised Ink Flag raised at Umm Rashrash, giving Israel access to the Red Sea.

It completed Israel's hold on the southern Negev and opened the route to the Red Sea. The almost bloodless advance ended with the improvised Ink Flag raised at Umm Rashrash, giving Israel access to the Red Sea.

slides.title: 1949 Armistice Agreements
slides.cap: 1949 armistice lines after agreements with Egypt, Lebanon, Jordan, and Syria
slides.body: The 1949 Armistice Agreements ended the main fighting between Israel and Egypt, Lebanon, Jordan, and Syria. the agreements confirmed survival: the state declared in May 1948 had endured invasion, expanded beyond parts of the UN partition plan, and gained internationally recognized ceasefire lines. These lines, later known as the Green Line, were not formal peace borders. They left major issues unresolved, including refugees, Jerusalem, and relations with neighboring Arab states. The agreements were armistices rather than peace treaties, but they confirmed that Israel had survived and established the Green Line as the practical boundary of the young state.

stats.lbl: It confirmed Israel's survival and created the political map that shaped decades of conflict.
